questions.challenge_mechanism: The rule that the work done in a cycle is the area enclosed by the loop is learned on loops that do not cross themselves, where there is one area and the sign is settled by the direction of travel. Here there are two lobes and they are traversed in opposite senses, so the net work is the difference between them and the device is an engine by 150 J rather than a refrigerator by 50 J. Adding the two areas is not a slip in arithmetic but a slip in what the word enclosed means once the boundary crosses itself: the gas does positive work on one leg of the smaller lobe and has more taken back on another.
questions.question:
A fixed mass of an ideal gas is taken round the cycle shown in the figure. Pressure is measured in $\mathrm{kPa}$ and volume in $\mathrm{dm^{3}}$, so an area on the diagram is measured in joules.

The cycle follows the path $A \to B \to X \to C \to D \to X \to A$, where $A$ is $(2,\,100)$, $B$ is $(2,\,300)$, $X$ is $(4,\,200)$, $C$ is $(5,\,150)$ and $D$ is $(5,\,250)$. Each leg is a straight line on the diagram. The gas therefore passes through the point $X$ twice and the path crosses itself there.

(a) Show that the work done by the gas on the legs $A \to B$ and $B \to X$ together is $500\ \mathrm{J}$, and that the work done on the leg $X \to A$ is $-300\ \mathrm{J}$.

(b) Show that the work done by the gas as it goes round the smaller lobe, $X \to C \to D \to X$, is $-50\ \mathrm{J}$.

(c) Hence determine the net work done by the gas in one complete cycle and state, with a reason, whether the cycle is that of a heat engine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the work done by the gas on the legs $A \to B$ and $B \to X$ together is $500\ \mathrm{J}$ and that the work done on the leg $X \to A$ is $-300\ \mathrm{J}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the work done by the gas as it goes round the lobe $X \to C \to D \to X$ is $-50\ \mathrm{J}$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence determine the net work done by the gas in one complete cycle and state, with a reason, whether the cycle is that of a heat engine.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Leg $A \to B$ is at constant volume, so no work is done (M1). On leg $B \to X$ the pressure falls linearly from $300$ to $200\ \mathrm{kPa}$ while the volume rises from $2$ to $4\ \mathrm{dm^{3}}$, so the work done by the gas is the mean pressure times the change in volume:

$$W_{BX} = \frac{300 + 200}{2} \times (4 - 2) = 250 \times 2 = 500\ \mathrm{J} \quad \text{(A1)}.$$

On leg $X \to A$ the pressure falls from $200$ to $100\ \mathrm{kPa}$ while the volume falls from $4$ to $2\ \mathrm{dm^{3}}$, so

$$W_{XA} = \frac{200 + 100}{2} \times (2 - 4) = 150 \times (-2) = -300\ \mathrm{J} \quad \text{(A1)},$$

negative because the gas is being compressed.

**(b)** On $X \to C$ the work done by the gas is $\tfrac{200 + 150}{2} \times (5 - 4) = 175\ \mathrm{J}$ (M1). Leg $C \to D$ is at constant volume, so no work is done. On $D \to X$ the volume falls, giving $\tfrac{250 + 200}{2} \times (4 - 5) = -225\ \mathrm{J}$. The total for the lobe is

$$175 + 0 - 225 = -50\ \mathrm{J} \quad \text{(A1)}.$$

**(c)** The larger lobe, $A \to B \to X \to A$, gives $0 + 500 - 300 = +200\ \mathrm{J}$ (M1). The net work for the whole cycle is therefore

$$200 + (-50) = 150\ \mathrm{J} \quad \text{(A1)},$$

positive, so over one complete cycle the gas does net work on its surroundings (A1). The cycle is that of a heat engine: it takes in heat, rejects less, and converts the difference into $150\ \mathrm{J}$ of work each cycle. Note that the net work is the *difference* of the two lobe areas, not their sum: the smaller lobe is traversed anticlockwise and undoes a quarter of what the larger lobe achieves.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for using the mean pressure on a straight-line leg, or equivalently for recognising that the work is the area of a trapezium; (A1) for 500 J; (A1) for -300 J. A candidate who integrates is equally acceptable but no faster. The mark for the zero on leg A to B is carried in the (M1): a candidate who gives a non-zero value for a constant-volume leg has misunderstood what the area represents.

(b) (M1) for the two non-zero legs; (A1) for -50 J. The sign is the point of the part and should be marked: -50 J and +50 J are different answers here, not a slip in convention, because the next part depends on which lobe undoes the other.

(c) (M1) for evaluating the larger lobe as +200 J; (A1) for the net 150 J; (A1) for the conclusion that it is a heat engine, which must be tied to the sign of the net work and not merely asserted from the word engine in the stem. Credit the observation that the net work is 150 J and not 250 J only where it is explained by the opposite senses of the two lobes.
questions.explanation:
The work done in a cycle is the signed area enclosed by the path, and a path that crosses itself encloses two areas with opposite signs. This is not a special case invented for the question: any self-intersecting closed curve on a $p$--$V$ diagram behaves this way, and the rule the candidate needs is the one they already have -- add up the work leg by leg and let the signs take care of themselves. What makes the item worth asking is that the *picture* suggests a single number. Two regions are shaded, both look enclosed, and the natural reading of the textbook sentence is to add them.

Once the leg-by-leg sum is done the physics is transparent. The gas does 500 J of work expanding from B to X and has 300 J taken back compressing from X to A, netting +200 J on the left. On the right it does 175 J expanding and has 225 J taken back, netting -50 J. The engine therefore works, but only just over half as well as the larger lobe alone would suggest, and a designer who read the diagram as 250 J would overestimate the output by two thirds. That is the practical reason the distinction matters, and it is also why the item asks for the conclusion in part (c) rather than leaving the number to speak for itself.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Context: an ideal gas in a classroom cycle rather than a refrigeration or Stirling cycle, so no background beyond the first law is needed. Given and asked: the vertices are given as coordinates in kPa and dm3 so that every area is a whole number of joules, and the candidate is asked for each lobe separately before being asked for the net, which forces the sign of each to be confronted. Reasoning chain: a final part asks for the engine-or-not judgement, so the sign has to be interpreted rather than reported.
provenance.resource_origin: US AP Physics and undergraduate thermodynamics: cycles whose p-V paths cross themselves, where the net work is the difference of the lobe areas

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Read the two shaded regions off the diagram, add 200 J and 50 J because the work done in a cycle is the area enclosed by the loop, and report 250 J.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: A self-intersecting loop is not one loop. The two lobes are traversed in opposite senses, so the smaller undoes part of the larger and the signed areas subtract; the word enclosed, learned on simple loops, silently means two different things here.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: 250 J, obtained by adding the two lobe areas and then concluding that the device must be a heat engine because the total enclosed area is large and positive.

verification.method: Every leg is recomputed from the trapezium rule and the two lobe totals and the net work are checked against the sum of the legs.
solution_skeleton: Read the five vertex coordinates from the figure and note that X is visited twice.
Evaluate the work on each of the five non-trivial legs using the mean pressure.
Sum the legs that make up the larger lobe to get +200 J.
Sum the legs that make up the smaller lobe to get -50 J.
Add the two lobe contributions to get the net work of 150 J.
Interpret the positive sign: net work is done by the gas, so the cycle is that of a heat engine.

questions.challenge_mechanism: Two intuitions collide and both are wrong. The first is that infinitely many bounces must take infinitely long; the second, its mirror image, is that a ball which stops after 4.5 s must have made some finite number of bounces. The resolution is that the flight times form a geometric sequence with ratio 0.8, whose sum converges, and that a convergent sum of infinitely many positive terms is exactly what 'comes to rest' means here. Nothing in the arithmetic is harder than summing a geometric series; what is hard is accepting that the answer to 'how many bounces' is not a number.
questions.question:
A ball is released from rest at a height of $1.25\ \mathrm{m}$ above a horizontal floor and falls freely. Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

Immediately after each bounce the speed of the ball is $0.8$ times its speed immediately before that bounce, and it leaves the floor vertically. The figure shows the velocity--time graph for the motion.

(a) Show that the interval between the first and second bounces is $0.8\ \mathrm{s}$, and that the intervals between successive bounces form a geometric sequence with common ratio $0.8$.

(b) Determine the time at which the ball stops bouncing.

(c) State how many bounces the ball makes before it stops, and explain how that is consistent with your answer to part (b).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the interval between the first and second bounces is $0.8\ \mathrm{s}$, and that successive such intervals form a geometric sequence with common ratio $0.8$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the time at which the ball stops bouncing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how many bounces the ball makes before it stops and explain how that number is consistent with the finite time found in part (b).

questions.answer:
**(a)** The speed just before the first bounce follows from $v^{2} = 2gh$: $v = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 1.25} = 5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ (M1). Just after that bounce the speed is $0.8 \times 5.0 = 4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ upwards, so the time to rise and fall back to the floor is

$$\frac{2u}{g} = \frac{2 \times 4.0}{10} = 0.8\ \mathrm{s} \quad \text{(A1)}.$$

Each bounce multiplies the speed by $0.8$ and the flight time is proportional to the speed, so each interval is $0.8$ times the previous one: the intervals are $0.8,\ 0.64,\ 0.512,\ \ldots$, a geometric sequence with common ratio $0.8$ (A1).

**(b)** The first fall takes $\tfrac{v}{g} = \tfrac{5.0}{10} = 0.5\ \mathrm{s}$ (M1). The total time is that first fall plus the sum to infinity of the bounce intervals:

$$T = 0.5 + \frac{0.8}{1 - 0.8} = 0.5 + 4.0 = 4.5\ \mathrm{s} \quad \text{(A1)}.$$

**(c)** Infinitely many (A1). The intervals form a convergent geometric series, and a convergent series of positive terms can have infinitely many of them: the partial sums approach $4.5\ \mathrm{s}$ from below and never exceed it. The model has no smallest bounce and no last bounce -- for every bounce there is a later one -- yet the total time is finite, because the time each bounce takes shrinks faster than the number of bounces grows (A1). The ball does not stop at the instant of a bounce: $4.5\ \mathrm{s}$ is the limit of the bounce times, and it is approached, not attained.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for the impact speed of 5.0 m/s from v-squared = 2gh or from an equivalent route; (A1) for the rebound speed 4.0 m/s and the flight time 0.8 s; (A1) for the statement that the flight time scales with the speed, so the ratio of successive intervals is also 0.8. A candidate who computes the second interval explicitly as 0.64 s and infers the ratio from that is creditable.

(b) (M1) for the 0.5 s first fall; (A1) for recognising the infinite sum and evaluating it as 4.0 s, giving 4.5 s in total. A candidate who adds a finite number of terms and rounds should not receive the second mark: the question asks when the ball stops, and the answer is the limit, not an approximation to it.

(c) (A1) for 'infinitely many'; (A1) for the explanation. The explanation must do more than repeat that the series converges -- it should say why that answers the apparent contradiction, namely that the number of terms and the size of their sum are different questions. Credit the observation that 4.5 s is a limit that is approached rather than an instant at which a bounce occurs.
questions.explanation:
This is Zeno's paradox wearing a kinematics costume, and it is worth asking because both halves of it are counter-intuitive to a candidate who has met geometric series only as a means of adding up a finite list. An infinite list of positive terms is expected to sum to infinity; it does not, and the reason is that the terms shrink in a fixed ratio.

The physics is doing real work here too. The rebound speed is a fixed fraction of the impact speed, the flight time is proportional to the speed, and so the times inherit the ratio 0.8 directly from the speeds. A candidate who reaches for the heights instead -- each rebound height is 0.64 of the previous one -- gets the same ratio after an extra step, since the time varies as the square root of the height. Either route lands on the same sum, and that is a useful thing to check: if the two routes disagreed, the model would be inconsistent.

What the item is really testing is whether a candidate can hold two facts at once: the motion has a definite end at 4.5 s, and it has no final bounce. Both are true, and the discomfort of holding them together is the difficulty.

provenance.adaptation: Three changes. Given and asked: the fraction is given as a speed ratio and the height is chosen so that the first fall takes exactly 0.5 s and the total is exactly 4.5 s, both whole numbers of tenths. Structure: the velocity-time graph is supplied so the candidate can see the intervals shrinking rather than only being told they do. Reasoning chain: a third part asks directly how many bounces occur, which the parent form leaves implicit and which is the whole point.
provenance.resource_origin: UK A-Level Mechanics: a ball rebounding to a fixed fraction of its previous height, and the total time of the motion as a geometric series

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Count the bounces until the rebound height becomes negligible, decide the ball makes about a dozen of them, and add up that many intervals to get a stopping time a little under 4.5 s.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The number of bounces is not a number and the stopping time is a limit, not a total of a counted list. The intervals form a geometric sequence whose sum converges, so infinitely many positive terms occupy a finite time, and no last bounce exists to be counted.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: About fourteen bounces and a stopping time near 4.4 s, obtained by truncating the sequence once the rebound height falls below a millimetre and treating the remainder as negligible.

verification.method: The impact speed, the first-flight time, each successive interval and the convergent sum are all recomputed, and the ratio is checked to be less than one so that the sum to infinity is valid.
solution_skeleton: Find the impact speed from the drop height using v-squared equals 2gh.
Apply the rebound fraction to get the speed after the first bounce.
Convert that speed into a flight time using 2u over g.
Argue that each interval inherits the ratio 0.8 from the speeds.
Add the first fall to the sum to infinity of the bounce intervals.
Conclude that the number of bounces is infinite while the total time is 4.5 s.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: C.4 Standing waves and resonance: boundary conditions, nodes and antinodes, the harmonic series of a string fixed at both ends. With C.2 Wave model: superposition of normal modes
questions.subtopic: C.4 Harmonics that cannot be excited because the plucking point is one of their nodes
questions.challenge_mechanism: The constraint is invisible until it is looked for. A string fixed at both ends can vibrate in any of its normal modes, and the usual question asks which frequencies are possible -- all of them. Plucking the string at a particular point adds a second condition which is not a condition on frequency at all: any mode that has a node at that point receives no energy, whatever its frequency. The candidate's task is to notice that the pluck position is a constraint and then to do something with it, which means asking where the nodes of the nth harmonic are and whether one of them falls at L/3.
questions.question:
A string of length $L$ is fixed at both ends and is plucked at a point one third of the way along it, that is at a distance $\tfrac{L}{3}$ from one end, as shown in the figure. The resulting vibration is a superposition of normal modes of the string.

(a) Show that the third harmonic has nodes at $x = \tfrac{L}{3}$ and $x = \tfrac{2L}{3}$, where $x$ is measured from one end.

(b) Hence determine which harmonics are absent from the vibration, giving your answer as a condition on the harmonic number $n$.

(c) Explain why a mode that has a node at the plucking point cannot be excited at all, and state which harmonics would be absent if the string were plucked at $\tfrac{L}{4}$ instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the third harmonic has nodes at $x = \tfrac{L}{3}$ and $x = \tfrac{2L}{3}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence determine which harmonics are absent from the vibration, giving a condition on the harmonic number $n$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a mode with a node at the plucking point cannot be excited at all, and state which harmonics would be absent for a pluck at $\tfrac{L}{4}$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The displacement of the $n$th harmonic has the form $y \propto \sin\!\left(\tfrac{n\pi x}{L}\right)$, which is zero when $\tfrac{n\pi x}{L} = k\pi$, so the nodes are at $x = \tfrac{kL}{n}$ for $k = 0,\,1,\,\ldots,\,n$ (M1). For $n = 3$ these are $x = 0$, $\tfrac{L}{3}$, $\tfrac{2L}{3}$ and $L$, so there are nodes at $\tfrac{L}{3}$ and $\tfrac{2L}{3}$ (A1).

**(b)** A node of the $n$th harmonic falls at $x = \tfrac{L}{3}$ when $\tfrac{kL}{n} = \tfrac{L}{3}$ for some integer $k$, that is when $n = 3k$ (M1). The absent harmonics are therefore those whose number is a multiple of $3$: the third, sixth, ninth and so on (A1).

**(c)** The amplitude of each mode in the superposition is set by how far the string is pulled aside at the plucking point in that mode (M1). If the pluck point is a node of the mode, the displacement there is zero for that mode at all times, so the pluck does no work on it and it receives no energy: the mode is absent entirely, not merely quiet. Plucking at $\tfrac{L}{4}$ instead would remove the harmonics whose number is a multiple of $4$ -- the fourth, eighth, twelfth and so on (A1), since $\tfrac{kL}{n} = \tfrac{L}{4}$ gives $n = 4k$.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for the node positions of the nth harmonic, or directly for the third harmonic from a sketch of three half-wavelengths; (A1) for both L/3 and 2L/3. A candidate who draws the mode and reads the nodes off their sketch is fully creditable -- the figure invites exactly that.

(b) (M1) for setting kL/n equal to L/3 and rearranging to n = 3k; (A1) for the condition stated in words or as a list. A list that stops at the third harmonic earns the method mark only, because the part asks for a condition on n.

(c) (M1) for the energy or amplitude argument; (A1) for the multiples of 4. Do not credit 'the string cannot move there, so that mode is damped': the mode is never started, which is a different claim, and the distinction is what separates an explanation from a restatement. Also accept a candidate who answers in terms of symmetry: a mode whose node sits at the pluck point is antisymmetric about that point while the initial displacement is not.
questions.explanation:
The pluck point is a constraint on the motion, and the interesting thing about it is that it constrains *shape* rather than frequency. A string fixed at both ends admits every harmonic; a string plucked at L/3 admits every harmonic except those that are already still at L/3. Nothing about the allowed frequencies changes -- the third harmonic is still a perfectly good mode of the string -- but it is not excited, and so it is not heard.

This is why a plucked string sounds different depending on where it is plucked, and why guitarists exploit it: plucking near the bridge produces a bright, thin tone because the low harmonics, whose nodes are widely spaced, are the ones most likely to have a node near the bridge and are thus the ones suppressed. The item is the simplest case of that, with a pluck point at a simple fraction of the length so that the condition on n comes out as divisibility.

The general statement is worth carrying away: for a pluck at L/m, the absent harmonics are the multiples of m. Part (c) asks for m = 4 so that the candidate can check the rule they have just derived against a second case and see that it was a rule and not an accident of the number three.

provenance.adaptation: Written against the C.4 bullet on the harmonic series of a string fixed at both ends. The pluck point is placed at a simple fraction of the length so that the condition on the harmonic number is divisibility by 3, which can be stated exactly and checked, and the figure shows the first three modes with the pluck point marked so that the third mode's node there can be seen rather than only calculated.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Decide that all harmonics are present because a string fixed at both ends admits every member of the harmonic series, and treat the plucking point as affecting only how loud the note is.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The pluck point is a second constraint, and it constrains shape rather than frequency. A mode with a node at the pluck point is never started, so the question is not which frequencies are allowed but which of the allowed ones receive any energy.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: All harmonics are present, with the third merely quieter than the others because the string is not moving much there at the moment it is released.

verification.method: The node condition is checked numerically for the sine profile of each harmonic and the divisibility rule is verified against the harmonics that are claimed to be present and absent.
assertions: all(approx(sin(3 * k * pi / 3), 0, 1e-9) for k in range(1, 6))
solution_skeleton: Write the displacement profile of the nth harmonic of a string fixed at both ends.
Find where it vanishes to get the node positions kL over n.
Set one of those positions equal to L over 3 and rearrange for n.
State the condition on n and list the harmonics it removes.
Explain in energy terms why a node at the pluck point means no excitation.
Repeat the argument for a pluck at L over 4 to confirm the rule.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A.3 Work, energy and power: work done by a force, conservation of energy. With A.2 Forces and momentum: resolution of forces on an inclined plane, friction
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.subtopic: A.3 The force needed to push a block up a ramp is greatest at an intermediate angle, while the work needed falls steadily as the ramp gets steeper
questions.challenge_mechanism: Force and work pull in opposite directions and the item asks about both. Raising the angle does two things at once: it increases the component of the weight along the slope, which raises the required force, and it shortens the slope for a given height, which lowers the work. Over most of the range both effects are present, so the answer to 'which ramp is hardest' depends on which word hardest means, and a candidate who answers one question and believes they have answered the other has walked into the only trap the item contains.
questions.question:
A block of mass $m$ is pushed at constant speed up a ramp of vertical height $h$, inclined at an angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the ramp is $\mu = 0.50$. The figure shows the ramp and a graph of the required force against $\theta$.

(a) Show that the force $F$, applied parallel to the ramp, that is needed to keep the block moving at constant speed is

$$F = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta).$$

(b) Determine the angle $\theta$ at which this force is greatest.

(c) Show that the total work done against gravity and friction together is

$$W = mgh\,(1 + \mu\cot\theta),$$

and explain why the work becomes smaller as the ramp gets steeper even though, for angles below your answer to part (b), the required force becomes larger. Take $m = 20\ \mathrm{kg}$, $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and $h = 3.0\ \mathrm{m}$ in your numerical illustration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that the force parallel to the ramp needed to keep the block moving at constant speed is $F = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the angle $\theta$ at which the force found in part (a) is greatest.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the total work done is $W = mgh(1 + \mu\cot\theta)$ and explain why it falls as the ramp steepens while the required force may rise.

questions.answer:
**(a)** At constant speed the resultant force along the ramp is zero, so the applied force balances the component of the weight down the slope and the friction: $F = mg\sin\theta + f$ (M1). The normal reaction is $R = mg\cos\theta$ and $f = \mu R$, so

$$F = mg\sin\theta + \mu mg\cos\theta = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta) \quad \text{(A1)}.$$

**(b)** Differentiate with respect to $\theta$:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}F}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = mg(\cos\theta - \mu\sin\theta).$$

Setting this to zero gives $\tan\theta = \tfrac{1}{\mu} = 2$, so $\theta = 63.4^{\circ}$ (M1) (A1). For $\mu = 0.50$ the second derivative is negative there, so it is a maximum: at $\theta = 30^{\circ}$ the force is $183\ \mathrm{N}$, at $63.4^{\circ}$ it is $219\ \mathrm{N}$ and at $90^{\circ}$ it is $196\ \mathrm{N}$, so the force rises and then falls again.

**(c)** The distance travelled along the ramp is $s = \tfrac{h}{\sin\theta}$, so

$$W = Fs = mg(\sin\theta + \mu\cos\theta)\frac{h}{\sin\theta} = mgh\left(1 + \mu\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right) = mgh(1 + \mu\cot\theta) \quad \text{(M1)}.$$

As $\theta$ increases, $\cot\theta$ decreases, so $W$ falls towards its limiting value $mgh$, the work against gravity alone (A1). Numerically, $W = 1098\ \mathrm{J}$ at $30^{\circ}$, $736\ \mathrm{J}$ at $63.4^{\circ}$ and $589\ \mathrm{J}$ at $90^{\circ}$. The two quantities move in opposite directions below $63.4^{\circ}$ because they are different things: the force is what the push must match at each instant, while the work is that force multiplied by a distance that shrinks as $\tfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$ as the ramp steepens. Between $30^{\circ}$ and $63.4^{\circ}$ the force grows by about 20 per cent while the distance falls by about a third, and the distance wins (A1).
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) (M1) for resolving along the ramp with zero resultant, (A1) for the normal reaction and the friction law. A candidate who omits friction on the grounds that the block is moving at constant speed has confused constant speed with zero friction and cannot be credited beyond the first mark.

(b) (M1) for differentiating and setting the derivative to zero; (A1) for 63.4 degrees. Stating that the answer is arctan(1/mu) without the differentiation earns the method mark only if the result is justified. The check that it is a maximum rather than a minimum may be done by citing the values at the ends of the range, which is the safer route for most candidates.

(c) (M1) for the substitution s = h over sin theta and the simplification; (A1) for the observation that cot theta decreases so the work falls monotonically; (A1) for the explanation in terms of force and distance moving in opposite directions. The third mark is for the explanation, not the arithmetic: a candidate who produces the formula and says nothing about the opposite movement has answered a different question.
questions.explanation:
The two halves of the item are individually straightforward and jointly surprising, which is the shape the whole wave is aiming at. Resolving forces on an inclined plane is early-year work; multiplying by the distance along the slope is one line. What is not obvious until it is written down is that the force has a maximum in the middle of the range at all -- most people expect the steepest ramp to be the hardest to push up -- and that the work has no such maximum.

The maximum in the force is worth dwelling on. At small angles the friction term $\mu mg\cos\theta$ dominates and falls as the ramp steepens; at large angles the gravity term $mg\sin\theta$ dominates and rises. The sum peaks where the two effects balance, at $\tan\theta = 1/\mu$, which for a rough surface is a shallow angle and for a slippery one is steep. That is a genuinely useful piece of design intuition: if you are choosing a ramp angle and the limiting factor is the force available, the worst choice is not the steepest one.

The work is a different quantity and behaves differently, and the whole point of part (c) is that a candidate's physical intuition about 'harder' has to be attached to one of the two before it means anything.

provenance.adaptation: Written against the A.2 and A.3 bullets on resolution of forces and work done. The coefficient 0.50 is chosen so that the maximum of the force falls at arctan(2) = 63.4 degrees, an angle outside the range most candidates will have met in a numerical example, and the numerical illustration is built so that the force rises by about 20 per cent over the range where the work falls by about a third.

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Decide that the steepest ramp is the worst in every respect, and either report the work as greatest at the steepest angle or look for the angle of greatest work without noticing that the question asked about force.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Force and work are not monotone in the same direction. The force peaks at arctan(1/mu) because the friction term falls while the gravity term rises, whereas the work is the force times a distance that shrinks as one over sin theta and decreases throughout.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: The work is greatest at 63.4 degrees, carried over from the answer to part (b) on the assumption that the hardest angle to push up must also be the angle that needs the most work.

verification.method: The stationary point, the force values at three angles and the work values at the same three angles are all recomputed, and the opposing movements of force and work are checked explicitly.
solution_skeleton: Resolve the weight along and perpendicular to the ramp.
Apply the friction law and write the required force.
Differentiate the force with respect to the angle and set it to zero.
Confirm the stationary point is a maximum by comparing with the ends of the range.
Multiply the force by the distance along the slope, h over sin theta.
Compare how the force and the work each change as the angle increases.
